problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

A. An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges, which are held fixed at a distance d. Imagine that we have two identical dipoles, which are oriented opposite to each other and are a distance r apart.

A1. When two dipoles interact, we take their potential energy U to be zero when they are at a large distance apart. On the basis of this assumption, express the potential energy of the system of the two dipoles as a function of q, d, r and the fundamental constants.

A2. Assume that $d \ll r$. Give an approximate expression for the potential energy as a function of q, d, r and the fundamental constants.

To answer the above question, use the binomial approximation $(1+x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ for $|x| \ll 1$.

B. During a high-energy physics experiment, two particles approach each other head-on with speed $\upsilon = 0.9520c$, as measured in the reference frame of the laboratory. What is the magnitude of the velocity of each particle with respect to the reference frame of the other particle?

Suppose that we have two reference frames: a frame S and a frame S′ which moves with constant velocity υ with respect to frame S. According to the Special Theory of Relativity, an event that happens at a point (x, y, z) at time t with respect to frame S will happen in reference frame S′ at the point (x′, y′, z′) at time t′.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2014-1-fig1.png

The coordinates of the event in the two reference frames are related through the following relations, known as the Lorentz transformations:

$$x' = \frac{x - \upsilon t}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\upsilon^2}{c^2}}} = \gamma\left(x - \upsilon t\right)$$

$$y' = y$$

$$z' = z$$

$$t' = \frac{t - \dfrac{\upsilon x}{c^2}}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\upsilon^2}{c^2}}} = \gamma\left(t - \frac{\upsilon x}{c^2}\right)$$

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

Two identical perfectly elastic spheres A and B of mass $m = 1\,\mathrm{kg}$ and radius $R = 2\,\mathrm{m}$ are placed on a smooth horizontal floor so that the centre of the first is at $x = 0$ and the centre of the second at $x = 120\,\mathrm{m}$, while the line joining their centres lies on the x axis. At time $t = 0$ we launch the spheres towards each other with speeds of magnitudes $\upsilon_{oA} = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\upsilon_{oB} = 6\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

1) Considering, as a first approximation, that their collision is instantaneous, calculate:

(a) the time $t_1$ of the collision,

(b) the position of each sphere ($x_1$ and $x_2$) when they collide

and, for times from 0 to $2t_1$, draw the graphs of the quantities:

(c) $x_A = f(t)$ and $x_B = f(t)$ on the same set of axes

(d) $\upsilon_A = f(t)$ and $\upsilon_B = f(t)$ on the same set of axes

(e) $F_A = f(t)$ and $F_B = f(t)$ on the same set of axes

(f) Comment on the shape of the graphs at times around the time $t_1$.

2) In a more realistic approximation, we assume that throughout the collision the interaction force between the spheres has a constant value equal to $F_o = 100\,\mathrm{N}$.

(a) Calculate the duration of the collision.

(b) Calculate the minimum magnitude of the velocity of each body during the collision, as well as the times at which it occurs. Do the velocities become zero simultaneously? Comment.

(c) Calculate the minimum distance between the centres of the two spheres.

(d) Assuming that the elasticity of the spheres manifests itself in a way similar to that of a spring, calculate the value of the equivalent spring constant k.

(e) Draw the diagrams of question 1 for the times corresponding to the duration of the collision.

3) Extending the analogy with the spring, we improve the model of the collision further by considering that the force varies linearly from the value 0, at the beginning of the collision, up to a maximum value (again $F_o = 100\,\mathrm{N}$) and then decreases linearly, until it vanishes, at the same rate in absolute value.

(a) What do you think the duration of the collision will be now? Prove your claim without performing numerical calculations.

(b) In terms of the data of the problem and the results so far, write the numerical expressions of the functions $F_A = f(t)$ and $F_B = f(t)$, $\upsilon_A = f(t)$ and $\upsilon_B = f(t)$, $x_A = f(t)$ and $x_B = f(t)$.

(c) Calculate the minimum distance of approach of the spheres.

(d) What is now the value of the equivalent spring constant k?

(e) Draw qualitatively the diagrams of question 2(e).

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

A negative charge of value $-q$ ($q > 0$) has been fixed to the right end of a horizontal spring of constant K. The left end of the spring is fixed to an immovable point. The charge can move only along the x axis. At a distance L from the right end of the spring, when the spring has its natural length, a linear distribution of positive charge of infinite length has been placed vertically, i.e. positive charges placed along a straight line ε. The x axis and the linear charge distribution lie in the same vertical plane. The linear distribution of positive charge of infinite length is characterised by the linear charge density λ, i.e. the charge per unit length, and produces an electric field with the following characteristics:

i) The direction of the electric field at a point A outside ε lies in the plane that is perpendicular to ε, passes through A and intersects ε at a point, say K. The direction of the field at A lies on the straight line through the points A and K, and its sense is from K towards A.

ii) The magnitude of the field is $E = K_{\text{ΗΛ}}\dfrac{2\lambda}{r}$, where $K_{\text{ΗΛ}}$ is the electric constant and r the distance AK.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2014-3-fig1.png

Placing the 0 of the x axis at the right end of the spring when the spring has its natural length, with L the point at which the x axis intersects ε, and considering the quantities K, $K_{\text{ΗΛ}}$, λ, q and L as known, answer the following questions:

1) Find the points $x_0$ on the x axis at which the charge q is in equilibrium, stating the condition that the known quantities must satisfy for such points to exist.

2) An equilibrium point is called stable if, when a body is at it and is displaced by small displacements from it, the body returns to the equilibrium position because of the forces acting on it. An equilibrium point is called unstable if, when a body is at it and is displaced by small displacements from it, the body does not return to the equilibrium position but moves away from that position because of the forces acting on it. Characterise the points of the previous question as stable or unstable.

(Hint: You may consider small displacements Δx from the points $x_0$ and use the approximation $(1+\alpha)^{\nu} \cong 1 + \nu\alpha$, where the quantities α and ν are positive or negative, while the quantity α is much smaller than one in absolute value, $|\alpha| \ll 1$.)

3) Under which conditions can the charge q perform simple harmonic motion? Calculate the restoring constant D of the oscillation in this case.

4) In which direction will the charge q initially move if it is released at some point x without initial velocity, in the case where the condition you found in question 1 is not satisfied?

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

Suppose that our world is governed by Classical Mechanics. In this "classical" universe we could try to "build" a hydrogen atom by placing an electron in a circular orbit around a proton. However, we know that a non-relativistic accelerated electric charge radiates energy at a rate given by the Larmor formula:

$$\frac{dE}{dt} = -\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{q^2\alpha^2}{c^3} \qquad \text{(cgs units)}$$

When we use cgs units, this means that we measure distances in cm, masses in g and time intervals in sec. In this system of units the electric constant $K_{\text{ηλ}}$ is dimensionless and has a value equal to one.

where q is the electric charge, α the magnitude of the acceleration and c the speed of light. Consequently, the classical atom has an obvious stability problem.

A. Show that the energy the electron loses in each revolution of the electron is small compared with the kinetic energy of the electron.

For this question, ignore the fact that the electron would follow a spiral orbit.

B. Use the typical size of an atom ($1\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}} = 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$) and of an atomic nucleus ($1\,\mathrm{fm} = 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$) and calculate the time $t_1$ in which the electron (whose orbit you must now consider to be a spiral) will fall onto the proton.

(Hint: The radius of the electron's orbit is a function of time. The solution of a differential equation of the form $r^2\,dr = \text{const}\cdot dt$ is obtained by integrating both sides as follows: $\displaystyle\int_{r_{\text{αρχ}}}^{r_{\text{τελ}}} r^2\,dr = \text{const}\int_0^{t_1} dt$)

C. Assuming that the electron moves in a circular orbit of radius $0.5\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ around the proton, compare its speed with the speed of light by calculating the ratio $\frac{\upsilon}{c}$. Then calculate the speed $\upsilon$ of the electron just before it falls onto the nucleus. Can this happen? Justify your answer.

D. As the electron approaches the proton, to what value does its energy $E$ tend? Is there a minimum value of energy that the electron can have?

The mass and the charge of the electron are given as $m_e = 9.1\cdot10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $q_e = -1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ respectively.

Problem 4. Experimental part

According to the Special Theory of Relativity, the total energy and the momentum of a particle moving at relativistic speeds (speeds close to the speed of light) are given by the relations:

$$E = K + m_o c^2 = \gamma m_o c^2 \qquad (1)$$

$$p = \gamma m_o \upsilon \qquad (2)$$

$$\text{with}\quad \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\upsilon^2}{c^2}}} \qquad (3)$$

where $m_o$ is the rest mass of the particle, $\upsilon$ its speed, $K$ its kinetic energy, $p$ its momentum and $E$ its total energy.

For the experimental determination of the speed of light, based on the relativistic expressions for energy and momentum, we use an experimental set-up with a source of β radiation and a detector that measures the momentum and the kinetic energy of the electrons emitted by the source.

A. Prove the relation $K = \sqrt{(pc)^2 + \left(m_0c^2\right)^2} - m_0c^2$.

B. What is the speed $\upsilon$ of a particle that has kinetic energy $K = m_0c^2$?

C. On the basis of the following table of experimental measurements, draw the appropriate graph and apply the Method of Least Squares (see Note 1) in order to determine the speed of light $c$ with its uncertainty (see Note 2).

$$\begin{array}{c|c} p^2/2K\ (\mathrm{J\,s^2/m^2})\ 10^{-30} & K/2\ (\mathrm{J})\ 10^{-14} \\ \hline 1.03289 & 1.504 \\ 1.06667 & 1.840 \\ 1.09333 & 2.080 \\ 1.12000 & 2.352 \\ 1.14667 & 2.592 \\ 1.15378 & 2.656 \\ 1.18933 & 2.976 \\ 1.22489 & 3.328 \\ 1.24800 & 3.536 \\ 1.26578 & 3.664 \\ 1.30667 & 4.032 \\ 1.33689 & 4.320 \\ 1.37600 & 4.640 \end{array}$$

D. How can you determine from the previous results the rest mass $m_o$ of the electron with its uncertainty?

Note 1: Suppose that we have measured N pairs of values of x and y and found the values $x_i$ and $y_i$, where $i = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, N$. If we know that x and y are related by

$$y = B\cdot x + A$$

we can calculate A and B and draw the straight line $y = f(x)$ using the formulas:

$$A = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i y_i)}{\displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\right)^2} \qquad\qquad B = \frac{\displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i y_i) - \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i}{\displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\right)^2}$$

and for the uncertainties δA and δB of A and B respectively:

$$\delta A = \sigma_y \sqrt{\frac{\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\right)^2}{\displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\right)^2}} \qquad\qquad \delta B = \sigma_y \sqrt{\frac{N}{\displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\right)^2}}$$

where for $\sigma_y$:

$$\sigma_y = \sqrt{\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - A - Bx_i)^2}{N-2}}$$

Note 2: Suppose that we have calculated the mean value x of a quantity and its uncertainty δx. If for a derived quantity $y$ we have $y = f(x)$, then the uncertainty $\delta y$ follows from the relation:

$$\delta y = f'(x)\cdot\delta x$$

where $f'(x)$ denotes the derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$.

problems.title: Problem C (Experimental)
problems.problem:
Problem C (Experimental)

The speed υ with which a wave propagates in a medium is related to the frequency f and its wavelength λ through the fundamental equation of wave kinematics:

$$\upsilon = \lambda\cdot f \qquad (1)$$

which could lead us to the (false) conclusion that it depends on λ and f. In reality the speed depends only on the properties of the medium in which it propagates. In the case, for example, of a stretched string, the speed depends on the force F with which the string is stretched and on the linear density μ (mass per unit length of the string). Theoretically, indeed, they are related by the relation:

$$\upsilon = \sqrt{F/\mu} \qquad (2)$$

The following figure describes a standing wave created on a stretched string of length L, fixed at its two ends. According to theory, the number of antinodes n that are formed is related to the wavelength λ by the relation:

$$\lambda = 2L/n \qquad (3)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2016-3-fig1.png

By combining relations (1), (2) and (3) we can express the frequency as:

$$f = (n/2L)\sqrt{F/\mu} \qquad (4)$$

In order to verify experimentally the validity of the above relations, a group of students carries out a series of experiments. The stretched string of the figure is fixed at one of its ends and at the other, via a pulley, it is stretched by a hanging mass. The string can be made to vibrate by a suitable oscillator, with frequencies that can be controlled by the students, so as to produce a standing wave along it.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2016-3-fig2.png

Experiment 1

The students hang a mass at the end of the string of length L. They vary the frequency with which the string vibrates so that a steady wave pattern (standing wave) with a different number of antinodes n is formed. For each frequency, they measure the wavelength and calculate its speed. Their data are presented in Table 1.

Table 1

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & \text{Number of antinodes } n & \text{Frequency (Hz)} & \text{Wavelength (m)} & \text{Speed (m/s)} \\ \hline 1 & 2 & 62.6 & 2.25 & 141 \\ 2 & 3 & 92.8 & 1.50 & 139 \\ 3 & 4 & 124.0 & 1.13 & 140 \\ 4 & 5 & 156.6 & 0.90 & 141 \end{array}$$

1. Draw the curve of the frequency as a function of the number of antinodes n (on the last page). What is the relation between the two variables? On the basis of the data of the experiment, is relation (4) verified experimentally?

2. Draw the curve of the speed υ as a function of the frequency f (Attention! calibrate the speed axis over a range of 0–200 m/s). State the conclusion to which the result of the graph leads us.

Experiment 2

The students vary the mass hanging from the end of the string of linear mass density μ = 0.00051 kg/m. Increasing the mass increases the force F with which the string is stretched. In each case, they choose a suitable frequency so that the string vibrates, creating a standing wave, with the same number of antinodes (e.g. n=2). The measured frequency, the wavelengths and the calculated speeds are shown in Table 2.

Table 2

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & \text{Mass (kg)} & \text{Frequency (Hz)} & \text{Wavelength (m)} & \text{Speed (m/s)} \\ \hline 5 & 0.5 & 65.9 & 1.5 & 99 \\ 6 & 1.0 & 93.6 & 1.5 & 140 \\ 7 & 1.5 & 114.4 & 1.5 & 172 \\ 8 & 2.0 & 131.9 & 1.5 & 198 \end{array}$$

The speed of the waves υ is related theoretically to the force F and the linear mass density μ by relation (2). On the basis of the data of the experiment, calculate the quotient F/μ and represent graphically the function $\upsilon^2$ as a function of the quotient F/μ (on the last page). Do the experimental results agree with the theoretical ones, as predicted by relation (2)? If not, what could the reasons be? Given $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Experiment 3

In experiment 3, the students replace the vibrating string each time. They keep the tension constant, F = 9.8 N, and the string is made to vibrate so as to form the same standing-wave pattern each time (e.g. n=2). For each string, they measure the linear density. The measured frequency, the wavelengths and the calculated speeds are shown in Table 3.

Table 3

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & \text{Linear density (kg/m)} & \text{Frequency (Hz)} & \text{Wavelength (m)} & \text{Speed (m/s)} \\ \hline 9 & 0.000345 & 112.0 & 1.5 & 168 \\ 10 & 0.000492 & 94.3 & 1.5 & 142 \\ 11 & 0.000695 & 79.1 & 1.5 & 119 \end{array}$$

The "experimental" speed of the wave was determined for each string from the frequency and the wavelength with the help of relation (1). Calculate and record the "theoretical" speed of the wave for each linear density, on the basis of the data for F and μ that are given and with the help of relation (2). Compare the corresponding values. Are there differences?

Attention! All the answers of the experimental problem are to be given on the last sheet, which you will attach to the answer book. As regards the graphs: calibrate the axes, give them titles and include the appropriate units on each axis.

A homogeneous rod of mass $M = 3\,\mathrm{kg}$ and length $\ell = 1.6\,\mathrm{m}$ is held at rest in a horizontal position. The rod can rotate about the hinge (O) without friction. The rod is released and, when it reaches the vertical position, its lower end A collides elastically with the body ($\Sigma_1$) of mass $m_1 = 1\,\mathrm{kg}$, which is at rest on a smooth horizontal plane.

Along the smooth horizontal plane there is a second body ($\Sigma_2$) of mass $m_2 = 1\,\mathrm{kg}$, which performs simple harmonic oscillation (S.H.M.), tied to one end of an ideal spring of constant $k = 400\,\mathrm{N/m}$, the other end of which is rigidly fixed, as in the figure. The axis of the spring is in the direction of motion of the body ($\Sigma_1$). The two bodies ($\Sigma_1$) and ($\Sigma_2$) collide head-on and elastically.

The total energy of oscillation of the body ($\Sigma_2$) before the collision is $E_{o\lambda,2} = 8\,\mathrm{J}$. At the instant of the collision, for the displacement of the body ($\Sigma_2$), $x \geq 0$ holds. It is given that at the position x the total energy of the S.H.M. performed by the body ($\Sigma_2$), after the collision with the body ($\Sigma_1$), has the largest possible value.

Calculate:

D1. The magnitude of the force that the rod receives from the hinge just before the collision with the body ($\Sigma_1$).

D2. The position at which the elastic collision between the bodies ($\Sigma_1$) and ($\Sigma_2$) took place.

D3. Do the two bodies (Σ1) and (Σ2) collide again? If so, determine the minimum time interval that elapsed from the first to the second elastic head-on collision of the bodies ($\Sigma_1$) and ($\Sigma_2$).

D4. What is the maximum potential energy that the rod will acquire after the twelfth collision of the bodies (Σ1), (Σ2) and the rod?

Take as reference level of (Σ1), (Σ2) and the rod the horizontal plane of the oscillation. Given: the moment of inertia of the rod about its centre of mass, $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{12}M\cdot\ell^2$, the acceleration of gravity $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $\eta\mu\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \eta\mu\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. The dimensions of the bodies ($\Sigma_1$) and ($\Sigma_2$) are considered negligible.

problems.problem:
Problem A

In your answer book, write the number of each statement and next to it the letter T if the statement is true and the letter F if it is false, without justification.

A1. In a damped oscillation the damping force is of the form $F = -b\upsilon$, and the damping constant $b$ is very small. The percentage decrease of the amplitude and the energy loss per period are constantly decreasing.

A2. In a forced oscillation with $\omega_{\varepsilon\xi} \neq \omega_{o}$, the energy that the driver supplies to the system during one period is converted into kinetic energy, potential energy and heat.

A3. A harmonic wave propagates along a string that coincides with the half-axis Ox; the wave is produced by a source that makes the end O of the string (reference point $x = 0$) oscillate with equation $y = A\eta\mu\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}t\right)$. The material point Γ of the string, located at the position $x_{\Gamma} = +4\lambda$, reaches the position $y = A\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ with $\upsilon > 0$ for the 1st time at the instant $\dfrac{33T}{8}$.

A4. A mass of ideal fluid flows in a pipe. At some instant its kinetic energy has increased by 180 J and its potential energy has decreased by 60 J. The energy supplied to the fluid because of the pressure difference is 240 J.

A5. The right end of a string of length L is rigidly fixed, while the left end performs S.H.M. of frequency f. The wave produced has wavelength $\lambda = 0.4\,\mathrm{m}$ and, combining with the wave produced by reflection, creates a standing wave with an antinode at the left end of the string. The minimum length the string can have is $L_{min} = 0.4\,\mathrm{m}$.

A6. A body rotating about a fixed axis has angular momentum of magnitude $L_0$. If we apply to the body a constant torque of magnitude $\tau$, then it accelerates and after a time $\dfrac{L_0}{2\tau}$ the magnitude of its angular momentum becomes $\dfrac{3L_0}{2}$.

A7. A hydraulic installation has a variable cross-sectional area. Through an inlet 1 of cross-section $A$ a liquid of density $\rho$ enters with speed $\upsilon$. Through an inlet 2 of cross-section $2A$ a liquid of density $\dfrac{\rho}{2}$ enters with speed $2\upsilon$. Inside the installation the two liquids mix perfectly, so that the resulting liquid leaves through an outlet of cross-sectional area $\dfrac{A}{2}$. The density of the outgoing liquid is $\dfrac{3}{2}\rho$.

A8. Two synchronous sources of harmonic waves $\Pi_1$ and $\Pi_2$ are on the surface of a liquid and perform simple harmonic oscillations with equations $y_1 = y_2 = A\eta\mu(2\pi f t)$. A material point M of the surface of the liquid is at distances $r_1$ and $r_2$ from the sources $\Pi_1$ and $\Pi_2$ respectively, with $r_1 > r_2$. For destructive interference at the point M, the frequency of the waves, which propagate with speed of magnitude $\upsilon$, must be $f = \dfrac{(2N+1)\upsilon}{2(r_1 + r_2)}$, with $N = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$

A9. Two identical spheres A and B, each of radius r, are on a horizontal floor. Sphere A rolls (without slipping) and collides head-on and elastically with sphere B, which is initially at rest. The percentage of the initial kinetic energy of sphere A transferred to sphere B in the collision is 100%.

A10. A homogeneous ring of mass M and radius R performs a compound motion along a moving horizontal runway, as shown in the figure. The runway moves with speed of magnitude $\upsilon_{\Delta}$. If the ring rolls without slipping, then the magnitude of the velocity of its point of contact with the runway is zero.

Problem B

B1. An open cylindrical vessel of cross-sectional area A contains water up to a height H. At its bottom it has a hole of area $A_1 = \dfrac{A}{3}$, closed with a stopper. The acceleration of gravity is g. At the instant $t = 0$ we instantaneously pull the stopper out of the hole and the water begins to flow out unhindered. Prove that the total time required for the vessel to empty is given by the relation $t_{o\lambda} = 4\sqrt{\dfrac{H}{g}}$. Neglect friction and the viscosity of the water.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-2-fig1.png

[6 marks]

B2. In an experimental procedure, from the ceiling of a rigid rectangular-parallelepiped metal cage we suspend an ideal spring of constant $k = 100\,\mathrm{N/m}$, to the free end of which a body of mass $m = 1\,\mathrm{kg}$ is tied. We hold the body so that the spring is at its natural length. We let the system fall freely from a height $h = 0.15\,\mathrm{m}$, as shown in the figure. The cage collides with the ground and is instantly brought to rest, while at that moment the body is left free to perform S.H.M. Calculate the maximum force that the cage receives from the spring. The acceleration of gravity is given, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-2-fig2.png

Consider that the force the cage receives from the ground at the moment of its collision with it does not affect the speed of the body.

[6 marks]

B3. A massless smooth plank OA of length l is tied at its end A to an ideal spring of constant k, the other end of which is suitably fixed to a small massless pulley that can move without friction on a horizontal guide, so that the spring always remains vertical. The other end O of the plank rests on a smooth horizontal plane, as shown in the figure. A small box of mass m is carried very slowly along the plank without friction, with the result that the vertical distance of the end A of the plank changes from H to h, with $H = 2h$. The system is in one and the same vertical plane. The minimum energy required to carry the body is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-2-fig3.png

(a) $mgh$

(b) $\dfrac{1}{2}mgh$

(c) $\dfrac{3}{2}mgh$

The acceleration of gravity g is given.

Choose the correct answer and justify your choice.

[6 marks]

B4. A homogeneous rod of length $\ell$ slides in a vertical plane so that its end A touches a smooth vertical wall, while its end B touches a smooth horizontal floor, as shown in the adjacent figure. For the magnitudes of the velocities of the two ends of the rod, prove that $\dfrac{\upsilon_B}{\upsilon_A} = \varepsilon\varphi\varphi$, where φ is the angle that the rod makes with the smooth horizontal floor at each instant.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-2-fig4.png

[6 marks]

B5. A small sphere of mass $m_1$, moving with speed of magnitude υ on a smooth horizontal plane, collides elastically and head-on with another, stationary sphere of mass $m_2 = 3m_1$, which is tied to the end of a vertical ideal spring of constant k that is at its natural length $\ell_0$, while the other end of the spring is rigidly fixed at the point O of the ceiling. The maximum allowed speed υ, so that after the collision the body of mass $m_2$ just loses contact with the horizontal plane at the instant when the deformation of the spring is maximum and the length of the spring $\ell$ has increased by 20% compared with its natural length, is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-2-fig5.png

(a) 2 m/s

(b) 4 m/s

(c) 6 m/s

Choose the correct answer and justify your choice.

The acceleration of gravity is given, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; the small ball of mass $m_1$ performs only translational motion, and if the small ball of mass $m_2$ performed S.H.M. at the end of the vertical ideal spring it would have angular frequency of oscillation $\omega = 6\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

[6 marks]

B6. A string consists of two different strings AΓ and ΓB, with lengths $\ell_1 = 0.6\,\mathrm{m}$ and $\ell_2 = 0.825\,\mathrm{m}$ respectively. A wave of frequency f is produced on the string; it propagates in the first piece of string AΓ with speed $\upsilon_1 = 200\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and in the second piece ΓB with speed $\upsilon_2 = 110\,\mathrm{m/s}$. A standing wave is formed on the string.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-2-fig6.png

(a) What is the minimum frequency with which the string, which is tied at its two ends, must vibrate so that a node is formed at the junction point (Γ) of the two strings?

(b) How many nodes are formed in total on the string AB then?

[6 marks]

problems.problem:
Problem C (Experimental)

A group of Grade 12 students, as part of their laboratory activities, carried out the laboratory exercise "Study of the motion of a body suspended from a vertical spring" with the following materials:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-fig1.jpg

• a complete stand
• a spring of constant $K_0$
• a weight of mass M (much larger than that of the spring)
• a distance sensor
• a force sensor
• a microcomputer
• a laptop with suitable software for processing experimental data.

While trying to assemble the set-up, they found that the spring was very long, and they decided to cut it in the middle, creating two identical springs.

They used one of them for their experimental study.

Thus they assembled the set-up of the picture.

They displaced the weight vertically from its equilibrium position and let it move freely.

With the help of their equipment they recorded, for 4 s,

• the displacement of the weight from its equilibrium position (Image 1)
• the resultant of the forces acting on the weight (Image 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-fig2.png

Image 1

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-fig3.png

Image 2

In the two Images below (3 and 4), the arrows show the values (t – x) at the corresponding points of the position–time graph.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-fig4.png

Images 3 and 4

1st Question.

(a) Is the path of the weight straight or curved? [1 mark]

(b) From the experimental data, can you conclude whether the motion is periodic, and why? [2 marks]

(c) If the motion is periodic, what is its frequency? [2 marks]

With the help of suitable software they made a mathematical fit of the position–time graph, and the following Image 5 resulted.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-fig5.png

Image 5

The data card that appeared informed the group that the position–time function, to an accuracy of two decimal places for the given data, is:

$$x = 0.04\,\eta\mu(6.62t + 3.94) \quad \text{in S.I.}$$

2nd Question.

Do you agree that the equation of motion of the weight is this one, and why? [5 marks]

ATTENTION:

• The Position–Time graph intersects the position axis at (-0.03 m, 0 s).
• In the calculations of various quantities small differences (in the decimal digits) may arise between the values you calculate and the values of the mathematical fit. This should not concern you; continue the processing with the values you calculated.
• All quantities are measured in S.I. units.

Next, the group of students constructed the Force–Position graph and fitted it mathematically.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-fig6.png

3rd Question.

Using the data of the mathematical-fit card and your theoretical knowledge, calculate the mass of the weight. [5 marks]

Finally, with the help of the processing software they constructed the graph of velocity versus displacement from the equilibrium position and fitted it mathematically.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2017-3-fig7.png

4th Question.

On the basis of the theoretical knowledge you have, justify the shape of the graph. [5 marks]

Of course, the group of students also answered other questions, and after the completion of the study their supervising teacher posed a problem.

5th Question.

Using the materials they have, could they force the weight to oscillate with a new frequency $f' = \sqrt{2}\cdot f$?

Give your own answer, explaining exactly what you would do and why. [5 marks]

Two similar thin, uniformly thick and homogeneous rods OA, OB, each of mass $M = 6\,\mathrm{kg}$ and length $\ell = 1\,\mathrm{m}$, are welded together at one of their ends O and form a right angle. The system of the two rods can rotate without friction about a horizontal axis perpendicular to the plane AOB, which passes through the end A of the system of the two rods. Problem A. Multiple-choice questions without justification

1. An observer "hears" the beats from the superposition of the sounds of two tuning forks with frequencies $f_1 = 2000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_2$, noting an intensity maximum every $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$. If $f_2$ is increased by $1\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the time between two successive zeros of the intensity increases. The frequency $f_2$ is:

(a) $2\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (b) $1998\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (c) $2000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (d) $2002\,\mathrm{Hz}$

2. On the surface of a liquid at rest, interference phenomena are observed from waves coming from the synchronous sources $\mathrm{O_1}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$. Let the circle $(\mathrm{O_1}, R)$ intersect the half-line $\mathrm{O_2}\varepsilon$ at the points A and B, which are points of constructive interference, while between A and B there is one more such point. The distance AB is equal to:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-1-fig1.png

(a) $\lambda$ (b) $2\lambda$ (c) $3\lambda$ (d) $4\lambda$

3. In the transmission system of a bicycle, the radii of the front and the rear gear are in the ratio $\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{3}{1}$, while those of the rear gear and the wheel are in the ratio $\dfrac{R_2}{R_3} = \dfrac{1}{10}$. If the pedals rotate with frequency $2\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the radius of the rear gear is $3\,\mathrm{cm}$ and the wheels roll without slipping, then the speed of the bicycle is:

(a) $3.6\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (b) $7.2\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (c) $10.8\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (d) $14.4\pi\,\mathrm{m/s}$

4. A small body is placed, and is in equilibrium, on the free upper end of a spring whose lower end is fixed at the base of a smooth inclined plane. The spring is compressed by $8\,\mathrm{cm}$. A second, identical body is placed in contact with the first. Until their first instantaneous stop, they will have travelled on the inclined plane a distance:

(a) $4\,\mathrm{cm}$ (b) $8\,\mathrm{cm}$ (c) $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ (d) $16\,\mathrm{cm}$

If the densities of water and mercury are $\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}$ and $\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}$ respectively, the height above its initial level to which the mercury rises in the right arm is:

(a) $\mathrm{H}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}$ (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}$ (c) $\dfrac{\mathrm{H}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}$ (d) $2\mathrm{H}\cdot\dfrac{\rho_{\nu\varepsilon\rho}}{\rho_{\upsilon\delta\rho}}$

6. Three spheres A, B, Γ of equal size and with masses $m$, $3m$, $4m$ respectively are at rest on a smooth horizontal plane, with B between A and Γ. Sphere A is launched with a velocity of magnitude $\upsilon$ towards sphere Γ. If all collisions are central and elastic, the total number of collisions that will take place is:

(a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4

7. If the point K, in the snapshot of the figure, has a vertically downward velocity while P is at rest, the wave is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-1-fig2.png

(a) standing

(b) travelling towards the right

(c) travelling towards the left

(d) the data are not sufficient for us to know

8. A body performs SHM with amplitude A. At the instants when the displacement from the equilibrium position is $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\mathrm{A}$, the ratio $\dfrac{U}{K}$ of the potential to the kinetic energy of the oscillation has a value equal to:

(a) $\dfrac{5}{3}$ (b) $\dfrac{9}{5}$ (c) $\dfrac{5}{4}$ (d) $\dfrac{5}{9}$

9. A wheel rolls without slipping on a horizontal terrace and, on reaching its edge, leaves it and falls. Considering the air resistance negligible, during the fall and until it reaches the ground the velocity of its lowest point has direction:

(a) vertically downwards

(b) horizontal, in the sense of the initial motion

(c) horizontal, opposite to the sense of the initial motion

(d) oblique

10. Two synchronous sources $\mathrm{O_1}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$, a distance $(\mathrm{O_1O_2}) = 10\,\mathrm{m}$ apart, produce waves on the surface of water, and interference phenomena are observed. The equation of oscillation of a point B of the straight segment $\mathrm{O_1O_2}$, which is the one closest to the midpoint M of $\mathrm{O_1O_2}$ that oscillates with maximum amplitude, is $y = -0.2\sin 2\pi(2t-2)$ (SI). The propagation speed of the wave is:

(a) $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (b) $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (c) $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (d) $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$

11. A homogeneous sphere rolls without slipping with a velocity of magnitude $\upsilon_{cm}$ on a smooth horizontal plane. At some instant it collides elastically with a smooth vertical wall and returns. The magnitude of the velocity of the lowest point of the sphere after the collision is:

(a) 0 (b) $\upsilon_{cm}$ (c) $2\upsilon_{cm}$ (d) $\sqrt{2}\,\upsilon_{cm}$

12. A material point performing SHM of period T and amplitude A covers a distance S in a time interval $\dfrac{T}{4}$. The maximum value of the distance ($S_{max}$) during the above time interval is:

(a) A (b) $\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{A}$ (c) $2\mathrm{A}$ (d) $(2-\sqrt{2})\mathrm{A}$

Inside the container there is an ideal liquid, and by some mechanism a constant pressure P is maintained. At some instant a small hole of area A opens in the container, and the liquid starts to flow out. The pressure continues to remain constant and equal to P. The force F exerted on the container because of the liquid flowing out is equal to:

(a) $\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{PA}$ (b) $\mathrm{PA}$ (c) $\dfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{PA}$ (d) $2\mathrm{PA}$

(a) $0.4\,\mathrm{m}$ (b) $0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ (c) $0.8\,\mathrm{m}$ (d) $1\,\mathrm{m}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-1-fig3.png

The air resistance is considered negligible and there is no friction in the axis of rotation of the door. If the moment of inertia of the door about the axis of rotation is $I = \dfrac{1}{3}ML^2$, the time it will need to close is:

(a) $\dfrac{\pi L(4M+3m)}{12m\upsilon}$ (b) $\dfrac{L(4M+3m)}{m\upsilon}$ (c) $\dfrac{\pi L}{2m\upsilon}\left(\dfrac{M}{3}+\dfrac{m}{4}\right)$ (d) $\dfrac{\pi L(4M+3m)}{2m\upsilon}$

If the speed of the ultrasound in the body amounts to $1540\,\mathrm{m/s}$, then the maximum speed of oscillation of the surface of the heart is:

(a) $2.57\,\mathrm{cm/s}$ (b) $2.57\,\mathrm{mm/s}$ (c) $25.7\,\mathrm{cm/s}$ (d) $0.257\,\mathrm{mm/s}$

At a point K of the elastic medium the two waves arrive, one wave having travelled a distance greater than the other by $\dfrac{5}{4}\lambda$, and they interfere with amplitude $\mathrm{A_1}$. We decrease the oscillation frequency of the sources by $\dfrac{1}{3}$ relative to the initial one, without changing their amplitude, and then the amplitude of oscillation of point K becomes $\mathrm{A_2}$. The ratio $\dfrac{\mathrm{A_1}}{\mathrm{A_2}}$ is equal to:

(a) 1 (b) $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (c) $\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$ (d) $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$

If the moment of inertia of the rod about an axis passing through its midpoint and perpendicular to it is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{12}ML^2$, then the distance x is equal to:

(a) $\dfrac{L}{2}$ (b) $\dfrac{2L}{3}$ (c) $\dfrac{3L}{4}$ (d) $\dfrac{L}{4}$

problems.problem:
Problem B

The scooter of the figure consists of a body and two identical wheels. The wheels are considered cylinders (not necessarily homogeneous) which rotate, without friction, about massless axles that are fitted to the body.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-2-fig1.png

[Labels in the figure: πλάγια όψη = side view; κάτοψη = top view.]

The axles are perpendicular to the wheels and pass through the centres of the wheels, which are also their centres of mass. The front axle is $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the centre of mass of the body, while the rear axle is $8\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the centre of mass of the body. Each wheel has mass $m = 0.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ and radius $R = 0.05\,\mathrm{m}$.

For the moment of inertia of the wheels, about the axles mentioned above, accept that $I = \lambda m R^2$, where $\lambda$ is a positive number.

The body has mass $M = 1.25\,\mathrm{kg}$; its shape is a parallelepiped with two gaps, where the wheels have been placed.

If we let the scooter move on an inclined plane of great length, with angle of inclination $\varphi$ ($\sin\varphi = 0.6$ and $\cos\varphi = 0.8$), without initial velocity, it descends along a straight path, and throughout its motion the wheels roll without slipping. We measured that in this motion the scooter needed $2\,\mathrm{s}$ to cover $9\,\mathrm{m}$.

A. Use the above data to calculate the value of $\lambda$.

B. Calculate the minimum value of the coefficient of static friction between the wheels and this inclined plane.

problems.problem:
Problem C. Experimental part

To measure time with the greatest accuracy we use digital timers that are triggered by special infrared-radiation sensors, the photogates. With these, and with the help of different modes of their operation, we can directly measure the times over which experimental processes evolve and indirectly calculate other physical quantities (such as time intervals, average velocity, instantaneous velocity, acceleration, etc.).

From the top of an inclined plane (Figure 1) a homogeneous cylindrical body of radius r is left to roll, without initial velocity. Let $\upsilon_{cm1}$ and $\upsilon_{cm2}$ be the velocities of the centre of mass of the body at the positions where the two photogates are located; the photogates are a distance $d = S_2 - S_1$ apart, as in the following figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-3-fig1.png

Figure 1. The experimental arrangement

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-3-fig2.png

Figure 2. The calculation of Δt

[Labels in the figures: φωτοπύλη 1, 2 = photogate 1, 2; Αρχική θέση κυλιόμενου σώματος = initial position of the rolling body; αρχή μέτρησης = start of measurement; τέλος μέτρησης = end of measurement.]

For the motion of the body from the first photogate to the second, the following relations hold:

$$\frac{1}{2}m\upsilon_{cm1}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega_1^2 + mgh = \frac{1}{2}m\upsilon_{cm2}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega_2^2 \quad (1)$$

$\upsilon_{cm1} = \omega_1 . r$ (2), $\upsilon_{cm2} = \omega_2 . r$ (3), $\upsilon_{cm2} = \upsilon_{cm1} + \alpha_{cm} . \Delta t$ (4), $d = \upsilon_{cm1} . \Delta t + \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha_{cm} . \Delta t^2$ (5)

By eliminating $\Delta t$ (the measurement of the time interval $\Delta t$ is achieved with the help of a system of 2 photogates and an electronic timer, and the time interval of the motion of the body from the first photogate to the second photogate, which is a distance d away, is calculated directly each time (see also Figure 2)) between equations (4) and (5), it follows that: $\upsilon_{cm2}^2 - \upsilon_{cm1}^2 = 2\alpha_{cm} . d$ (6)

From relations (1), (2), (3) and (6) the relation $\alpha_{cm} . d\left(1+\dfrac{I}{mr^2}\right) = g . h$ (7) follows,

so that $\alpha_{cm} = \dfrac{g}{\left(1+\dfrac{I}{mr^2}\right) . d} . h$ (8)

From relation (8) we find that the acceleration of the centre of mass of the rolling body is proportional to the vertical distance between the two positions of the body (i.e. of the 2 photogates). The graph of the function $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$ is a straight line (Figure 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2019-3-fig3.png

Figure 3. The graph $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$

If we define as $K = \dfrac{g}{\left(1+\dfrac{I}{mr^2}\right)d}$ the slope of $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$, then by solving the last relation for I it follows that: $I = mr^2\left(\dfrac{g}{K . d} - 1\right)$ (9)

That is, for certain values of h we must calculate the corresponding values of the acceleration of the centre of mass of the cylinder and construct the graph of $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$.

The difference in height (h) between the two photogates is calculated from the formula $h = d . \dfrac{H}{L}$ (since $\sin\varphi = \dfrac{h}{d} = \dfrac{H}{L}$, or because of the similarity of triangles), where: $d = S_2 - S_1$ is the distance between the photogates along the inclined plane, $L = 0.365\,\mathrm{m}$ is the total length of the inclined plane and H is the reading of the electronic distance meter for each position of the inclined plane, after the reference plane has first been made horizontal (with a spirit level) ($H = 0$).

To calculate the acceleration of the centre of mass of the cylinder, we take $t = 0$ to be the instant at which we release the body from the top of the inclined plane without initial velocity, $t_1$ the instant at which the body passes through the first photogate, having been displaced from its initial position by $S_1$, and $t_2$ the instant at which the body passes through the second photogate, having been displaced from the top of the inclined plane by $S_2$. For $S_1$ and $S_2$ the following relations hold:

$S_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha_{cm}t_1^2$ (10)

$S_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha_{cm}t_2^2$ (11)

We solve relations (10) and (11) for $t_1$, $t_2$, subtract them side by side, and the relation $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\alpha_{cm}}} . \left(\sqrt{S_2} - \sqrt{S_1}\right)$ follows, from which the final relation is easily deduced:

$\alpha_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{\Delta t^2}\left(\sqrt{S_2} - \sqrt{S_1}\right)^2$ (12)

Required apparatus:

Multi-purpose inclined-plane apparatus, electronic distance meter.

Electronic timer and accessories (photogates, power supply).

Metal cylinder of diameter $10\,\mathrm{mm}$.

Electronic balance, distance meter, vernier caliper, spirit level.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE

First we measured the mass and the radius of the cylinder and recorded the values in the table below (given to you). We placed the two photogates on the plane. With the spirit level we found the position at which the inclined plane is horizontal and we zeroed the electronic distance meter ($H = 0$).

We measured the distance of the photogates from the top of the inclined plane and recorded the values $S_1$, $S_2$ in the Table of the answer sheet.

We activated the electronic timer in the appropriate measurement mode (when the body passes through the photogates the timer will record the time interval $\Delta t$ of the motion from the first photogate to the second (Figure 2)).

We then raised the inclined plane by a small amount H and recorded the value of the electronic distance meter in the table below.

We let the cylinder roll from the top of the inclined plane and recorded the reading of the electronic timer in the table below.

We repeated the measurement for five different inclinations of the inclined plane in total and recorded the readings of the distance meter (H) and of the timer ($\Delta t$) in the Table of the answer sheet.

[Table of the answer sheet (page 2 of the answer sheet), with the values as printed:]

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline m\ (\mathrm{kg}) & r\ (\mathrm{m}) & S_1\ (\mathrm{m}) & S_2\ (\mathrm{m}) & d = S_2 - S_1\ (\mathrm{m}) & L\ (\mathrm{m}) \\ \hline 0.0426 & 0.005 & 0.10 & 0.25 & 0.15 & 0.365 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{No.} & H\ (\mathrm{m}) & h = d.\dfrac{H}{L}\ (\mathrm{m}) & \Delta t\ (\mathrm{s}) & \alpha_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{\Delta t^2}.\left(\sqrt{S_2}-\sqrt{S_1}\right)^2\ (\mathrm{m/s^2}) \\ \hline 1 & 0.01 & 0.00411 & 0.6996 & 0.138 \\ \hline 2 & 0.02 & & 0.4522 & \\ \hline 3 & 0.03 & & 0.3710 & \\ \hline 4 & 0.04 & & 0.3136 & \\ \hline 5 & 0.05 & & 0.2822 & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

1. Calculate the value of the acceleration (to an accuracy of 3 decimal digits) with the help of relation (12) and fill in the appropriate column in the Table of the answer sheet.

2. Using the relation given to you, also fill in the column h of the Table of the answer sheet (to an accuracy of 5 decimal digits).

3. Draw on the mm paper of the answer sheet the graph of the function $\alpha_{cm} = f(h)$ from the values of the table that you filled in.

4. From the position of the 5 points on the graph, calculate the slope K of the straight line of the graph and, from relation (9), also calculate the experimental value of the moment of inertia of the cylinder (take $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$).

5. Calculate the theoretical value of the moment of inertia of the cylinder and the relative error with the help of the relation: $\sigma = \dfrac{\left|I_{\theta\varepsilon\omega\rho} - I_{\pi\varepsilon\iota\rho}\right|}{I_{\theta\varepsilon\omega\rho}}.100\%$

problems.title: Problem D. Experimental problem: study of the SHM of a mass–spring system
problems.problem:
Problem D. Experimental problem: study of the SHM of a mass–spring system

FIELD OF INVESTIGATION:

1. Excitation of a mass–spring system to perform SHM.

2. Investigation of the relation between the characteristic quantities of the oscillating system and those of SHM.

3. Taking measurements in order to calculate the value of the spring constant k and of the mass $m_\varepsilon$ of the spring, and to verify the validity of the principle of conservation of energy.

PREREQUISITE KNOWLEDGE:

A uniform metal cylinder of mass m attached to the free end of a spring can be set in motion after an additional extension or compression of the spring is produced; the spring is suspended from a fixed point with its axis vertical.

Ignoring every other force except the weight of the body and the elastic force of the spring, we can show that the motion of the body is described by the equation $x(t) = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + \varphi)$ (1), which also identifies the motion as SHM with angular frequency ω and period

$$T = 2\cdot\pi\cdot\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{K}} \qquad (2)$$

The periodicity of SHM is ensured by the fact that when the time is increased by $\dfrac{2\cdot\lambda\cdot\pi}{\omega}$ (λ a natural number), (1) does not change form, since:

$x\left(t + \dfrac{2\lambda\pi}{\omega}\right) = \mathrm{A}\sin\left\{\omega\left(t + \dfrac{2\lambda\pi}{\omega}\right) + \varphi\right\} = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + 2\lambda\pi + \varphi) = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + \varphi)$.

Relation (2) holds in the case of a massless spring (ideal spring). In practice, however, and as a rule, the mass of the spring $m_\varepsilon$ is of the same order of magnitude as the mass m of the body, so if it is not ignored it will appear in the expression for the period.

It can be shown that: $T = 2\cdot\pi\cdot\sqrt{\dfrac{m + \dfrac{m_\varepsilon}{3}}{k}}$ or $T^2 = \dfrac{4\cdot\pi^2}{k}\cdot m + \dfrac{4\cdot\pi^2}{3\cdot k}\cdot m_\varepsilon$, i.e. the equation $T^2 = f(m)$ is linear, of the form $\mathbf{T^2 = a.m + b}$, if we set $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathbf{4\pi^2}}{\mathbf{k}}$ (slope of the straight line) and $\mathbf{b} = \dfrac{\mathbf{4\pi^2}}{\mathbf{3k}}\,\mathbf{m_\varepsilon}$ (point of intersection with the $T^2$ axis).

We can therefore measure the period T of the oscillations of the system for different values of the mass m and, from the graph, calculate the values of the characteristics k and $m_\varepsilon$ of the spring.

EXPERIMENTAL PART

We experiment with an arrangement that includes a vertical spring suspended from a fixed point, with the possibility of hanging different masses on its free end. When the system is excited, and for a short time interval it is considered to perform SHM, the position of the mass as it moves along the vertical axis can be detected by a transmitter–position (distance) sensor placed below the mass, on the axis of its motion.

The transmitter locates the position x of the oscillating mass at every instant t and sends the data to a computer, where, after their collection and analysis by special software, the graph $x = f(t) = \mathrm{A}\sin(\omega t + \varphi)$ is displayed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2021-4-fig1.jpg

Each time a different mass m is used, which is set into SHM of amplitude about $20\,\mathrm{cm}$, so that from the corresponding graph the period is calculated as the time difference $t_2 - t_1$ between two successive peaks of the x–t curve.

problems.problem:
Problem D. Study of the electromagnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

EXPERIMENTAL PART

THEORY

Consider a straight conductor of length L carrying an electric current I. If the conductor is placed in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ with its direction perpendicular to the field lines, an electromagnetic force is expected to be exerted on it, as the resultant of the forces exerted by the magnetic field on the moving electric charges.

Suppose that carriers (e.g. free electrons), each with electric charge q, moving with velocity $\upsilon$, travel the length of the conductor in time Δt; then: $L = \upsilon\cdot\Delta t$ and $\sum q = I\,\Delta t$, therefore $L = \upsilon\dfrac{\sum q}{I}$ or $\sum q\cdot\upsilon = L\cdot I$ (1).

The electromagnetic (Lorentz) force exerted by a magnetic field on an electric charge moving perpendicular to its field lines is given by the relation $F = B\upsilon q$; therefore the corresponding macroscopic force on the conductor, because of (1), will have magnitude $F_L = \sum F = B\upsilon\sum q = BIL$ and is known as the Laplace force.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE

The determination of the characteristics of the Laplace force is attempted with the experimental procedure described here.

An electric circuit is set up, as shown in the figure, which includes as power supply a source of constant (DC) voltage 24 V in series with a rheostat, through which the current can be varied. Connected in series in the circuit is a straight conductor (a wire), which passes, without touching, between the poles of a horseshoe magnet placed on the pan of an electronic balance. The direction of the conductor is perpendicular to the field lines of the uniform magnetic field.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-4-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-4-fig2.png

Initially the circuit is open, so the reading of the balance, which is the normal force $\mathrm{N}_o$, is equal to the weight of the magnet $W_o = m_o g$, and is therefore proportional to its mass $m_o$. If we close the switch, depending on the polarity of the source and hence on the direction of the electric current in the conductor, the reading of the balance will change, showing an "apparent" weight $W$, which will be equal to the new normal force $\mathrm{N} = W_o \pm F_L'$, where $F_L'$ is the electromagnetic force exerted by the straight current-carrying conductor on the magnet. In essence, the magnitude of this force, which is added to or subtracted from the weight of the magnet, is equal to the magnitude of the force $F_L$ exerted by the magnet on the current-carrying conductor, as an action–reaction pair. The aim of the experiment is to take measurements for various values of the length of the conductor that lies inside the magnetic field and of the electric current, in order to relate the magnitude of the force $F_L$ to the length $L$ of the conductor and the current I flowing through it.

TAKING MEASUREMENTS

To simplify the calculations, let us take the directions of the field lines and of the current as in the figure, so that the magnitude of the force $F_L$ is added to the weight $W_o$ of the magnet, and therefore the reading of the balance increases. Let us note here that the balance measures force, but is calibrated so that its reading equals the mass.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/greece-2022-4-fig3.png

With the switch open we note the reading of the balance, $m_o = 260\,\mathrm{g}$, which corresponds to the weight of the magnet $W_o = m_o g = 260\cdot10^{-3}\cdot 9.81\,\mathrm{N} = 2.55\,\mathrm{N}$.

We close the switch and adjust so that the current has the value $I = 1\,\mathrm{A}$ for each value of the length of the conductor, from $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ to $10\,\mathrm{cm}$, that we choose each time to lie inside the magnetic field. For each value of this length we note the reading of the balance and record the results in Table 1:

TABLE 1

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Conductor} & \text{Length } L\ (\mathrm{cm}) & \text{Current } I\ (\mathrm{A}) & \text{Balance reading } m\ (\mathrm{g}) \\ \hline \mathrm{L1} & 1 & 1 & 260.102 \\ \mathrm{L2} & 2 & 1 & 260.205 \\ \mathrm{L3} & 3 & 1 & 260.307 \\ \mathrm{L4} & 4 & 1 & 260.407 \\ \mathrm{L5} & 5 & 1 & 260.510 \\ \mathrm{L6} & 6 & 1 & 260.612 \\ \mathrm{L7} & 7 & 1 & 260.715 \\ \mathrm{L8} & 8 & 1 & 260.817 \\ \mathrm{L9} & 9 & 1 & 260.918 \\ \mathrm{L10} & 10 & 1 & 261.020 \end{array}$$

We repeat the measurement procedure, choosing a particular fixed length of the conductor $L = 4.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ and adjusting so that the current I takes various values from $0.2\,\mathrm{A}$ to $2\,\mathrm{A}$. For each value of the current we note the reading of the balance and record the results in Table 2:

TABLE 2

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Conductor} & \text{Current } I\ (\mathrm{A}) & \text{Length } (\mathrm{cm}) & \text{Balance reading } (\mathrm{g}) \\ \hline \mathrm{I1} & 0.2 & 4 & 260.082 \\ \mathrm{I2} & 0.4 & 4 & 260.164 \\ \mathrm{I3} & 0.6 & 4 & 260.245 \\ \mathrm{I4} & 0.8 & 4 & 260.325 \\ \mathrm{I5} & 1.0 & 4 & 260.408 \\ \mathrm{I6} & 1.2 & 4 & 260.490 \\ \mathrm{I7} & 1.4 & 4 & 260.571 \\ \mathrm{I8} & 1.6 & 4 & 260.652 \\ \mathrm{I9} & 1.8 & 4 & 260.734 \\ \mathrm{I10} & 2.0 & 4 & 260.815 \end{array}$$

PROCESSING THE MEASUREMENTS

For each "reading" $m$ of the balance, because of equilibrium, $\mathrm{N} = W_o + F_L$ or $mg = m_o g + F_L$ or $(m - m_o)g = F_L$ or $F_L = \Delta m\cdot g$.

TABLE 3

The neutral particles we can distinguish indirectly, from the processing of the data of the charged particles.

Suppose that in a detector we see the decay:

$$\mathrm{K}^o\rightarrow\pi^{+}+e^{-}+\ldots$$

that is, the decay of the neutral kaon $\mathrm{K}^o$ into a positively charged pion $\pi^{+}$ and an electron $e^{-}$. The dots indicate that there may also be other particles which, if they are neutral, we do not see in the detector. The trajectories of the particles are perpendicular to the field lines of a homogeneous magnetic field of intensity $\vec{B}$ with direction from the page towards the reader, whose cross-section is a square ΑΓΔΕ of side $\dfrac{5\alpha}{4}$, where $\alpha$ is a constant length.
